groups.generated-positive: Produced by synthesize-scenarios.ts and kept as written.
groups.generated-positive-rewritten: Produced by the generator, failed the one-step bar as phrased, rewritten so the deliverable is a call rather than a fact.
groups.label-corrected: Produced by the generator as should_trigger=false; label flipped after judging it against the skill body and the description.
groups.gap-register: GAP TEST. Wordiness, sentence length, active voice. The 971-char description hooks this half with 'tightening the plain wording'. Phrased in a user's vocabulary, not the skill's.
groups.gap-vocabulary: GAP TEST, split out of gap-register at the team lead's direction because it is a distinct sub-capability with a distinct status: the skill's register section requires taking the reader's nouns from the project rather than importing a synonym, and NO clause in the description hooks it. The only row testing it.
groups.gap-rejection: GAP TEST. Schema bounds and a rejected or silently non-rendering call. The old description wrongly excluded these as 'debug a schema error or a hang'; that fragment is gone, but nothing yet names the schema bounds POSITIVELY, so these match only on 'Composes the AskUserQuestion call itself'. Labelled true either way: the team lead's ruling is that firing on them is correct behaviour. Whether the group measures a new hook or the residual depends on the description SHA live at run time, which will be recorded.
groups.bounding-negative: Added at the team lead's direction, one per capability the 971-char description newly claims. Each is same-domain with a different deliverable, so a widened positive surface has something to be measured against. Recall without precision is not no-gaps.
groups.gap-comparability: GAP TEST. The description covers how a label and a description divide the work, but not whether options line up against each other on the same axes, order and units.
groups.gap-cost: GAP TEST. The description covers the recommendation's justifying fact, but not that every option description owes a cost, risk or foreclosure.
groups.gap-evidence: GAP TEST. The description says nothing about naming a gap in your own evidence inside the call.
groups.generated-negative: Hard negative produced by the generator and kept.
groups.generated-negative-sharpened: Generator negative, rephrased to sit harder on the neighbour that owns it.
groups.added-negative: Added by hand. Covers a declared exclusion or a neighbour the generator left uncovered.
groups.review-a-draft: DECISION GROUP, added to settle one question rather than to test a clause. The team lead holds an open commitment to the user on a deliberately-left gap — 'check this call over before I send it' — and closing it costs about 18 characters that the 1002-char description does not have to spare twice over. These two rows decide whether that spend is needed. Index 52 carries a pasted call; index 53 does not, and index 53 is the one that matters, because the pasted form is already covered — index 4 fired 3/3 against a description with no review hook at all. A FIRE ON INDEX 53 MEANS THE GAP IS ALREADY CLOSED and the 18 characters stay unspent. A decline on 53 with a fire on 52 localises the gap precisely to the no-paste phrasing, which is the only case worth paying for.
groups.author-eleven: The skill author's eleven scenarios, derived from the artifact independently of the generator and of the gap tests above. Expanded here with a file path, the person's situation, mixed casing and typos. Scored as its own group. A failure to fire belongs to the description, not to the query.

items.note: Clears the one-step bar (a call is multi-step to compose) but is the least specific query in the set: no file path, no backstory, generic 'auth flow'. Closest thing here to the documented 'Format this data' anti-pattern.
Seven items forces reasoning about independence, the 4-question cap and sequencing. Rich concrete detail.
Re-pitch, which the description claims explicitly. 'Both look the same to me' also lands on the comparability failure mode.

Effectively a cost-half gap query the generator found by reading the body. Caveat: 'what's the discipline here' can read as asking for house conventions, which the description excludes, so a non-fire is ambiguous between the gap and that negative clause. The gap-cost group is phrased to avoid that confound.

Pasted defective call with at least five independent faults: weak question text, 34-char header against a 12-char chip, an authored 'Other', non-distinguishing labels, no descriptions, no recommendation. Deliverable is unambiguously a fixed call.
Reading-answers capability, which the description claims. Borderline on the one-step bar: a terse expert answer is one sentence, but the licensing judgement is not a lookup.
Decide-whether-to-ask, claimed by the description's 'including the decision not to ask'. Lockfile detail gives it the evidence texture the bar wants.

Original: 'how do i signal a default? i put ... and they clearly never saw it'. FAILED the one-step bar — answerable in two sentences from one fact (no recommended field; ordering plus the ' (recommended)' token). Rewritten to carry three real options and ask for the call back, which makes it a reorder-plus-mark-plus-move-the-justification job.

Original: 'can i just take that as a yes and go ahead'. FAILED the one-step bar twice over — a yes/no question whose answer is the single fact 'a skip is not consent'. Rewritten so it also has to produce the replacement call.

Original: 'does that combo work'. FAILED the one-step bar — a yes/no whose answer is the single gotcha that a preview on a multiSelect is discarded in silence. Rewritten to demand the working call, so the model has to split into a sequence.

Generated as should_trigger=false. Flipped to true: a value only the reader can supply is a named case in the skill body, and the description's 'including the decision not to ask' claims it. Scoring a correct fire as a false positive would have penalised the description for working.
Over-long question in nested-clause style. User vocabulary: 'wall of text', 'nobody's going to read it'.

Three synonyms for one thing, with a docs/glossary.md that settles it. The 971-char description hooks plainness but never the project's own nouns, so this is the one row testing a clause that does not exist. A non-fire here is the cleanest attributable finding in the set.
Passive voice and future-perfect tense, quoted verbatim so the fault is in the query rather than described.
Three options each described on a different axis. User vocabulary: 'apples and oranges', 'can't line them up'.
Same axis, inconsistent units and one option silent on it. The 'same units' half of the rule.
Names the consequence rather than the rule — scanning does not surface the difference — which is how a user would arrive at this.
Deliverable is the rewritten call, which keeps it clear of the house-conventions negative that index 3 risks.
The specific case the skill body calls out: writing the cost of your own recommendation as plainly as the others.
The 'no honest bad choice' shape, plus the failure it causes — a reader who cannot recognise a mistake they have already made.
The skill's own worked example (unrun test suite), phrased as a user would, including the where-does-it-go question.
Unchecked evidence that could invalidate one option outright, plus the reason people omit it.
Weakest of this group: stale-fact framing brushes against 'the fact justifying it', which the description does claim, so a fire here is less clearly attributable to the gap than 20 or 21.
Open premise plus a three-way library comparison as the deliverable. Complex, multi-step, squarely in domain, output is a document.
Sits directly on the skill's own equivalent-options rule, and asks for a rationale rather than a call. Nasty in the right way.

discernment-nudge territory (shares answer, question, recommendation, reply). Sharpened from the generator's vaguer 'make sure they're not just taking my word for it' to the neighbour's actual deliverable: follow-up questions appended to a draft.
project-artifact territory (shares decision, question, sequence, state). Deliverable is a status page.

pptx territory, and pptx is the one neighbour the sweep flags as using pushy phrasing, so this is where displacement is most likely. Vocabulary collision is excellent: layout, text not reading, option comparison.
The wider-job exclusion after the answer has landed. Quotes the skill's own example label, which is what makes it tempting.

Replaces a generated academy-guide negative ('how do i get claude to remember our conventions') that was WEAK — thin vocabulary overlap and an obvious one-step answer, so nothing was ever routing here. This one is squarely in domain with a curriculum as the deliverable, and academy-guide's description is itself pushy ('Stop and check this skill before finishing any reply').

Covers the description's 'a guide, a cheat sheet, house conventions, a checklist' clause, which the generated negatives left entirely uncovered. This shape is one of the three queries description-writing.md records as actually discriminating.
Covers 'interviewing for requirements' from the wider-job clause. Maximum collision: a requirements interview is literally one question to the user at a time.

NOT FLIPPED, a deliberate departure from a direct instruction, raised to the team lead. The instruction's reasoning — that a schema-rejection query is in scope — is accepted and acted on at indices 49-51. But this row is not a schema-rejection query. It is 'building a TUI host', 'renders the dialog', 'canUseTool callback', 'over a websocket', 'one call in ten hangs with no dialog', and its deliverable is a working integration. It sits on TWO surviving fragments of the third exclusion, 'render the dialog' and 'fix a broken host or SDK integration', and it is verbatim the integration-case replacement negative the same instruction offered. Flipping it would inject a known-wrong label, the fault we agreed pollutes a measurement in both directions. No separate replacement negative is needed: this row already is one, and the new wording makes it sharper than before.

Covers 'build a survey or a form, or page through many items' — uncovered by the generated set. NOTE: the 965-char description dropped the trailing 'which enumerates rather than decides' that used to close this clause, so this row now tests a shorter negative than when it was written.
Pairs with index 11 (gap-register 1). Two independent derivations of the same intent, different phrasing — a phrasing-robustness check rather than a duplicate.
Pairs with index 13 (gap-register 3). Theirs comes at it through a reader who could not follow it; mine through the passive-voice original.
No skill vocabulary by design. Jargon half of the register, aimed at a non-engineer reader.
Pairs with index 14 (gap-comparability 1) and the constructions are near-identical though derived independently — the strongest single piece of corroboration in the cross-check.
Pairs with index 16 (gap-comparability 3). Both frame it as the consequence — scanning does not surface the difference — rather than as the rule.
Pairs with index 17 and index 3. No skill vocabulary by design.
Pairs with index 19. 'What they are giving up' is the foreclosure half rather than the cost half proper, which makes it the better-aimed of the two.
Pairs with index 20, again near-identical independently. My indices 21 and 22 extend the same capability to skimmed docs and a stale figure.

I covered this in substance at indices 1 and 9 but never as a marked gap test. This is the pure form and the crispest test of the new 'the layout' hook. Expanded so it is genuinely multi-step: multiSelect for the regions plus a second question for the order.

The bare intent 'what layout should I use' is close to a one-step lookup, so it is expanded with two rendered variants the reader must see — which is the preview path, and gives the query somewhere to go.

Pairs with index 6. Worth noting the author's finding: 'ask' is filtered as description boilerplate, so this capability reduces to ['decide','whether'] and no phrasing built on the word could clear a capability reading. That is a property of the inventory tool, not of the description.
Bounds 'options that compare and show their costs'. Deliverable is a comparison table in a review deck. Same axes, same vocabulary, different artifact.
Bounds 'what you have not checked'. Deliverable is an assumptions-and-risks log for a wiki. This is the newest positive clause and had nothing holding it.

Bounds 'tightening the plain wording'. Deliverable is a house style guide. Distinct near-miss from index 30's cheat sheet: that one aims at option labels, this one at the plain-language rule itself, so the two are not one negative written twice.

Bounds 'rewriting a question nobody could answer'. Grading calls against a rubric is the documented residual class — description-writing.md records it as the leak that survived a negative-space rewrite because it sits almost exactly on that clause. Phrased fresh rather than carried over from the retired fork's set.
Five questions and six options against hard bounds of 1-4 and 2-4. Deliverable is a call that fits, so it is a split-and-group job rather than a lookup.
A 48-character header against a 12-character chip, plus two identically-labelled options against the uniqueness constraint the body now names. Deliverable is the fixed call.

The pasted-call form. Expected to fire: index 4, a close variant, fired 3/3 against the 998-char description with no review hook. If this declines while index 4 held, that is variance rather than a gap.

The no-paste form, and the only row whose verdict changes a decision. Names a file rather than pasting content, so nothing in the query except the intent can carry it. Fires means the 18-character hook is unnecessary and the headroom stays; declines means the spend is justified with evidence rather than guessed at.

The sharpest row in the set and the one to read most carefully. A call that renders nothing with no error is what the removed fragment used to exclude; the query anchors itself to the composing side explicitly — 'not an sdk thing', 'something im doing in the call itself' — so it tests the boundary the third exclusion was just redrawn around. The skill body supports it: a preview over 2000 characters is withheld, a whitespace-only preview is dropped, and a preview on a multiSelect is discarded in silence, all of which render nothing without erroring. If this fires and index 32 does not, the redrawn boundary works.

install_state_observed.why_both_guards_missed_it: assert-skill-absent.ts sweeps four roots (~/.claude/skills, ~/.claude/plugins/marketplaces, ~/.claude/plugins/repos, <projectDir>/.claude/skills) for a SKILL.md answering to the name. These plugins are registered by config, and the cache directory ~/.claude/plugins/cache/ACMElabs/ask-user-question/0.0.1/skills/ask-user-question/ holds only a .gitkeep with no SKILL.md — so a content sweep of those roots finds nothing while the loader still serves the skill. OLD_NAMES uses a find bounded to -maxdepth 3 under two roots, which cannot reach it either. Neither guard consults `claude plugin list`, which TRUSTWORTHINESS 1.1b already prescribes as the complementary check on the grounds that 'a manifest on disk and a loaded plugin are different facts'.

mine_only: PROJECT VOCABULARY (index 12). The skill's register section has two halves — write plainly, and then use the project's own nouns rather than importing a synonym. The author's three register scenarios are all the first half. The 965-char description hooks the first half with 'tightening the plain wording' and says nothing about the second, so this remains an unhooked sub-capability and index 12 is the only row testing it.

SAME UNITS (index 15). Comparability is same axes, same order, same units. The author's scenarios 4 and 5 are the axes half. Index 15 is the units half: one option in minutes, one in vague prose, one silent.

COST OF YOUR OWN RECOMMENDATION (index 18). The skill body requires the recommended option's cost to be written as plainly as the others. The author's scenarios 6 and 7 are the general case; index 18 is the specific one people actually get wrong.
